header: For the petitioner(s) Mr. Muhammad Rashid Khan Dirma
For the State Mr. Sohail Khan Mandew, AAG.
body: AURANGZEB J.- Through this criminal revlsion petition under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Cr.P.C.), the petitioner has called in question the order d,aled 25.02.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-VI/MCTC, Bannu, in the trial arising out of FIR No'912 dated 03.11.2O2O, registered under sections 3021324 PPC at Police Station Saddar, District Bannu, whereby his application seeking the personal appearance of the complainant, Mst' Zulfishah, before the learned trial Court at Bannu for recording her statement was dismissed.

2. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that the FIR was registered on the report of respondent No'2, who is the complainant as well as the star witness of the prosecution, against the petitioner and co-accused Saifoor' During the trial, respondent No.2 moved an application seeking permission to record her statement through video link on the ground that she apprehended threats to her life at Bannu, particularly from her uncle, Saifoor Sikandri, who is an accused in the connected cross-case. The petitioner averred in his application that the defence had no objection to the recording of her statement through video link. It was, however, pointed out that the complainant had never appeared before the Court despite Mr. Muhammad Anwar Maidad Khel, Advocate repeated processes; that at one stage she claimed to be residing in Canada, but subsequently admitted before the Court that she was working as a lecturer at Peshawar; and that she had also attended a marriage ceremony at Serai Naurang, District Lakki Marwat, and visited her house at Bannu while her applications for recording evidence through video link were pending.

3. The learned trial Court, vide order dated 10.0l.2026, allowed the application of respondent No.2 for recording her statement through video link. The defence counsel raised no objection to the proposed arrangement. Thereafter, a request was transmitted through the proper channel to the learned District and Sessions Judge, Peshawar, who accorded permission for the purpose. Accordingly, on 15.01.2026, the complainant became available through the video-link facility at the Sessions Courts, Peshawar, while the prosecutor, counsel for the complainant, the petitioner and his counsel were present before the learned trial Court at Bannu' During the recording of her examination-in-chief, the defence counsel raised an objection that someone was providing instructions to the witness. It was further alleged that although the complainant was shown sitting under the supervision of a presiding officer at Peshawar, whenever she forgot something, four advocates standing near the rostrum prompted her. According to the petitioner, this circumstance was also noticed by the learned trial Court. The impugned order, however, records that the prosecutor and counsel for the complainant denied the allegation. Thereafter, the defence counsel and the petitioner left the courtroom, and the statement of the witness could not be recorded.

4, Subsequently, the petitioner moved an application seeking a direction for the personal appearance of the complainant before the learned trial Court at Bannu for recording her evidence. The prosecution and counsel for the complainant opposed the application on the ground that tJle complainant apprehended serious threats to her life at Bannu' It was also contended that the learned trial Court had no jurisdiction to review its earlier order dated 10.07.2026 in view of section 369 Cr.P.C. The learned trial Court, relying upon J section 369 Cr.P.C. and the judgment in Muhammad Shareef v. The State 11997 P.CI.L.J. 11951, held that its earlier order dated 10.01.2026 }.ad attained the status of a judgment and could not be reviewed, particularly when no clerical or arithmetical error had been pointed out. Consequently, the application was dismissed vide order dated 25.02.2026. It was, however, observed that the petitioner could nominate a representative or engage a lawyer of his choice to remain present at the place where the evidence was to be recorded through video link and witness the proceedings. The petitioner was also permitted to inform the learned trial Court about the availability of a video-link facility at Peshawar or Nowshera' Learned counsel for the complainant had stated before the learned trial Court that the complainant was ready and willing to record her statement from either the Sessions Courts, Peshawar, or Nowshera.

5. The petitioner has challenged the impugned order on the grounds that the right of cross-examination is a valuable and indispensable right of an accused; that the complainant, being the star prosecution witness, cannot be permitted to depose through video link in the circumstances of the present case, particularly when the same advocates were allegedly providing her with notes and prompting her during the proceedings; that the threats apprehended by the complainant were allegedly from her uncle and not from the petitioner; and that a person who could attend a marriage ceremony at Serai Naurang and visit her own house at Bannu, where the accused also resides, could conveniently appear before the learned trial Court. It was further contended that section 369 Cr'P'C' was not attracted to an interlocutory order of the nature under consideration. The petitioner, therefore, sought setting aside of the impugned order and a direction for summoning respondent No.2 in person for lecording her statement before the learned trial Court.
6. Arguments have been heard and the available record has been examined.

7. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the right of an accused to cross-examine a prosecution witness constitutes an essential component of a fair trial. According to him, although the initial permission for recording the complainant's statement through video conferencing was not opposed by the defence, the subsequent conduct of the witness gave rise to a genuine apprehension that she was being prompted or assisted by persons present at the remote location. It was submitted that, once such an objection was raised, the learned trial Court was required to examine the circumstances and ensure that the witness was deposing independently, without any outside influence or assistance.

8. Conversely, learned counsel appearing for the respondents supported the impugned order and submitted that the complainant was appearing from the Court of the learned District and Sessions Judge, Peshawar, under judicial supervision. It was argued that the recording of evidence through video conferencing is recognized by law and that the petitioner had been afforded an opportunit5r to cross-examine the witness. The leamed trial Court, therefore, rightly declined the request for her physical appearance and directed the defence to proceed with the cross-examination through the available video-link facilitY.
g.

The controversy involved in the present petition is not whether evidence can, in law, be recorded through video conferencing. The real question is whether the procedure adopted by the learned trial Court adequately protected the accused's right to a fair trial, particularly when an objection was raised during the recording of evidence that the witness appeared to be receiving instructions or prompting from unidentified persons at the remote location.

10. The right to a fair trial and due process is guaranteed under Article 10-A of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973. This constitutional guarantee is not confined to the formal conduct of judicial proceedings; rather, it requires that every party be afforded a real and effective opportunity to present its case, challenge the evidence produced against it and participate meaningfully in the proceedings. In a criminal trial, the right of an accused to cross-examine prosecution witnesses is an indispensable component of this constitutional protection. Such an opportunit5r must be real and effective and cannot be reduced to a mere procedural formality.

11. The Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, recognizes the importalce of oral evidence and the right of a party to test the veracity of a witness through cross-examination. Articles 2, 130, 131, t32, L33, t36, 137, 138, 140, t4t, 143, 144 and 15 1 , read together, provide the relevant framework governing the examination of witnesses, the order of examination, crossexamination and re-examination, the scope of questioning and the circumstances in which questions may be put to a witness to test his or her credibility. Cross-examination is not an empty formality; rather, it is an important instrument for discovering the truth, exposing inconsistencies and testing the accuracy and reliability of testimony. Its effectiveness depends upon the circumstances in which the witness is examined and the opportunity afforded to the opposing party to challenge the statement.

12. Article 164 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, as substituted by section 12 of the Criminal Laws (Amendment) Act,2023 (Act XXXVI of 20231, recognizes the use of modern devices and techniques for the purposes of evidence. It enables the Court to allow evidence to be recorded through modern devices, including video calls and video conferencing. The legislative recognition of modern technologr reflects the need to facilitate judicial proceedings, improve access to justice and overcome practical difficulties that may otherwise impede the recording of evidence.

13. The introduction of modern technologr, however, does not dilute the fundamental requirements governing the recording of evidence. Although the mode of recording may change, the essential safeguards relating to the identity, independence and credibility of a witness, as well as the right of an accused to effectively cross-examine such witness, remain intact. Article 164 must, therefore, be interpreted harmoniously with Article 10-A of the Constitution and the other provisions of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order governing the examination of witnesses. The use of technologr is a means of facilitating the administration of justice and cannot be permitted to become a source of prejudice to either party.

14. The relevant provisions of the Code of Crimina,l Procedure, 1898, also require consideration. Section 353 Cr.P.C. provides the general rule regarding the presence of the accused during the recording of evidence. Although the provision contemplates the recording of evidence in the presence of the accused or, where his personal attendance has been dispensed with, in the presence of his pleader, the concept of presence cannot be interpreted in a manner that ignores subsequent technological developments. Where an effective video-link arrangement enables the accused and his counsel to see and hear the witness, follow the proceedings and conduct cross-examination, such presence may, in appropriate circumstances, be treated as constructive or virtual presence. Nevertheless, the arrangement must ensure meaningful participation and must not cause prejudice to the defence.

15. Sections 354 to 363 Cr.P.C. regulate different aspects of recording evidence in criminal trials, including the manner of recording, the direction and supervision of the presiding Judge, the reading over of evidence and the recording of the demeanour of witnesses. These provisions demonstrate that the recording of evidence is a judicial function which must remain under the direction and control of the Court. The adoption of video conferencing does not relieve the trial Court of its responsibility to supervise the process and ensure that the evidence is recorded in a fair, transparent and reliable manner.

16. Sections 503 and 505 Cr.P.C. also provide a statutory mechanism for recording evidence through a commission where the attendance of a witness before the Court cannot conveniently be procured. These provisions reflect the legislative recognition that, in appropriate circumstances, evidence may be recorded through an alternative procedure without dispensing with the safeguards available to the parties. The opportunity of examining, cross-examining and reexamining a witness whose evidence is recorded through such a process remains an important consideration. The underlying principle is that an alternative mode of recording evidence cannot deprive either party of the opportunity to test the testimony of the witness.

17. Section 540 Cr.P.C. further empowers the Court to summon, examine, recall or re-examine any person whose evidence appears essential to the just decision of the case. The provision reinforces the duty of the trial Court to ensure that evidence necessary for a just decision is properly brought on record. Where any doubt arises regarding the manner in which evidence has been recorded, the Court may exercise its lawful powers to take appropriate corrective measures.

18. The question of recording evidence through video conferencing came under consideration before the august Supreme Court in Meera Shafi v. Ali Zafar IPLJ 2023 SC 3271. The august Supreme Court examined the concept of presence under section 353 Cr.P.C. and recognized that, in appropriate circumstances, presence may include constructive presence through video conferencing. The Court also examined Article 164 of the Qanun-e-shahadat Order, 1984, and recognized the utility of modern technology in judicial proceedings. It acknowledged that the law should not be interpreted in a manner that unnecessarily obstructs the use of technological facilities where the purpose of judicial proceedings can effectively be achieved through such means.

L9. The principle emerging from the above judgment is that physical presence is not an inflexible requirement in every case, provided the arrangement adopted by the Court preserves the essential safeguards of a fair trial' The purpose of crossexamination is to assist the Court in discovering the truth by testing the accuracy, consistency and credibility of testimony. The presiding Judge is required to remain vigilant and supervise the proceedings effectively. The right of crossexamination, although fundamental, must be exercised within the framework of law and cannot be treated as an unrestricted licence to conduct proceedings in any manner.

20. The august Supreme Court also recognized that the necessity and extent of safeguards may depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Where a genuine apprehension exists that a witness may be under the influence of, or tutored by, another person, the Court may require additional measures to ensure the independence of the testimony. Conversely, unnecessary procedural requirements should not be imposed in every case in a manner that defeats the very object of facilitating access to justice through modern technolory.

21. The matter was also considered by this Court in Muhammad r v. The State nd another IPLD 2O2ra Peshawar lOS). In that case, this Court examined the recording of evidence through video conferencing in criminal proceedings and recognized the possibility of recording evidence through modern technological means, subject to appropriate safeguards' The judgment emphasized that the identity of the witness, the circumstances in which the evidence is recorded, the presence or absence of other persons at the remote location and the effective exercise of the right of cross-examination are matters requiring judicial attention.

22. The safeguards discussed in Muhammad Israr (supra\ are intended to ensure that a witness is not tutored' prompted, coerced, induced or otherwise influenced while giving evidence. The Court must be satisfied that the witness is present at an authori zed and appropriate location, that his or her identity has been verified and that the arrangement enables the Court and the parties to observe and hear the witness clearly. The judgment further underscores that the use of technolory cannot be allowed to undermine the safeguards which ordinarity operate when a witness appears physically before the Court.

23,. The legal position emerging from the above judgments is that evidence recorded through video conferencing is not inherently unlawful or inadmissible merely because the witness is not physically present before the trial Court' At the same time, the adoption of such a mode does not confer unrestricted discretion upon the Court to record evidence without observing the safeguards necessary to protect the rights of the parties. The Court must ensure that the process remains transparent, reliable and subject to its effective supervision.

24. The matter has now received a specific procedural framework through the Peshawar High Court Virtual Court Proceedings Rules, .2026, framed in exercise of the powers conferred under Articles 202 and 203 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, L973, and notified vide Notification No.99-J12026 dated 11.03.2026, published in the official Gazette on 05.05.2026. The preamble of the Rules reflects the intention of this High Court to introduce, formulate and streamline a reliable and consistent mechanism for virtual Court proceedings and the purposeful use of modern technologies and devices in judiciat proceedings' The Rules are intended to facilitate the administration of justice through technological means. without compromising the independence' impartiality, credibility and solemnity of judicial proceedings' 2io. Rule 1 deals with the title, application and commencement of the Rules. Sub-rule (2) provides that the Rules shall apply to such Courts or classes of Courts, including Tribunals or proceedings, as the High Court may notify in this behatf, whereas sub-rule (3) provides that the Rules shall become applicable from the date of their publication in the oflicial Gazette. It is, therefore, necessary to distinguish between the commencement of the Rules and their applicability to a particular Cpurt, class of Courts or proceedings' Accordingly, the learned trial Court must ascertain whether the relevant Court and category of proceedings have been brought withinthenotifiedscopeoftheRulesbeforeapplyingtheir provisions to the present proceedings' 26. Rule 2 defines the expressions used in the Rules' Of particular relevance to the present controversy are the expressions "Court Point', 'Virtual Court Point"' "Virtual Assistant", "Real-time LinlC, "Proposed Person" and 'Telecommunication Faciliq/. A Court Point means the courtroom or place. where the Court is physically convened, whereas a Virtual Court Point is the place where a person is required to appear through a video link. The expression "Virtual Assistant" refers to a person nominated to supervise the virtual proceedings at the Court Point and the Virtual Court Point in accordance with the Rules and Schedule-8. Similarly, a Realtime Link includes a live television link, audio-video electronic means or other arrangements through which a witness is permitted to remain present online. These definitions demonstrate that virtual proceedings are not intended to be conducted through. an informal or uncontrolled electronic arrangement; rather, they contemplate designated locations, authorized supervision and an identifiable mechanism for communication between the two ends.

27. Rule 3 provides that expressions not delined in the Rules shall have the meanings assigned to them under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, the General Clauses Act, 1897, t}:,e Khyber Pakhtunkhwa General Clauses Act, 1956, and other applicable laws. Thus, the Rules must be read harmoniously with the existing procedural and evidentiary laws. They do not displace the statutory requirements governing the examination of witnesses in criminal proceedings. 2a. Rule 4 is the principal enabling provision concerning the virtual conduct of judicial proceedings. Sub-rule (1) permits a Court or Tribunal, subject to the law for the time being in force, to conduct proceedings virtually through audiovideo telecommunication facilities, modern devices and a conference platform. Sub-rule (2) empowers the Court, either on its own motion or on the request of a party or proposed person, to permit a virtua:l hearing where the attendance of the proposed person, whose examination appears essential to the just decision of the case, cannot be obtained without undue delay or unreasonable expense, or where extraordinary circumstances or sufficient cause make such an arrangement necessary in the interest ofjustice.

l1 29. Rule 4 further provides a procedural mechanism for seeking permission for virtual proceedings. Under sub-rule (3), the request is to be submitted on the prescribed form contained in Schedule-A, along with the prescribed Court fee, wherever applicable. Sub-rule (4) requires adequate notice of the application to the other parties and an opportunity of hearing before an appropriate order is passed. Under sub-rule (5), the Court is required to consider, inter alia, whether the request is intended to impede the trial or delay the proceedings and the costs associated with the virtual arrangement' More importantly, sub-rule (7) specifically deals with criminal cases and provides that, where the person to be examined is a prosecution witness, Court witness or defence witness, the counsel for the prosecution or defence, as the case may be' shall confirm readiness and proceedings and the time, place and technical facility for such proceedings. This requirement places a corresponding responsibility upon the party concerned to provide the necessary particulars so that the Court may make an informed judicial assessment before permitting the evidence to be recorded through such means.

30. Sub-rules (l2l and (14) of Rule 4 are also significant. They expressly provide that all proceedings conducted virtually shall be judicial proceedings and that the legal formalities prescribed under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order' 1984' and other applicable laws shall continue to apply' mutatis mutandis, as they apply to proceedings conducted physically' Consequently, the facility of video conferencing does not create an exception to the ordinary rules of criminal procedure or evidence. It merely provides an alternative means of conducting proceedings while retaining the substantive and procedural safeguards applicable to an ordinary trial' 31. Rule 5 prescribes the minimum facilities recommended for conducting virtual Court proceedings' These include computers or other suitable devices' unintermpted power supply, c€uneras, display units, microphones' speakers' to the Court willingness the location of the Person, his to be examined through virtual sound mixers, document visualizers, adequate lighting, proper seating arrangements ensuring privacy and the availability of a quiet and secure space. Sub-rule (2) further authorizes the adoption of modern electronic technologies and devices, subject to maintaining the independence, impartiality and credibility of judicial proceedings. The relevance of this provision to the present case is that the recording of evidence through a video link must take place in an environment that enables the Court to observe the witness and ensures that the proceedings are conducted without interference or compromise to the integrity of the testimony.

Rule 6, which deals with preliminary measures, is particularly relevant where a witness is to be examined from the Court of another district' Under sub-rule (1), there shall be a Virtual Assistant both at the Court Point and at the Virtual Court Point. However, the presence of a Virtual Assistant at the Virtual Court Point is specifically required where a witness or an accused person is to be examined' Sub-rule (2) provides for the nomination of persons by the High Court or the concerned District and Sessions Judge to perform the functions of Virtual Assistants in the district judiciary, whereas sub-rule (3)
requires that the Virtual Assistant at the Virtual Court Point must be a person falling within the categories prescribed in Schedule-B.

33. Schedule-B is of particular significance in the present case. It specifically provides that, where the proposed person is appearing from a Court falling within the jurisdiction of another district, the Virtual Assistant at the Virtual Court Point shall be an authorized official nominated by t-Ile concemed District and Sessions Judge' Thus' where a prosecution witness is to be examined from the Court of the learned District and Sessions Judge, Peshawar' the arrangement must be supervised by an authorized offrcial nominated by the concerned District and Sessions Judge' The mere presence of the witness within the premises of a judicial establishment is not sufficient to establish compliance with this requirement. The identity, nomination and responsibility of the VirtualAssistantmustbeascertainablefromthejudicialrecord. l3 3'4. Rule 6 further prescribes the responsibilities of the Virtual Assistant at the remote location. Under sub-rule (8), the Court must ensure that no unauthorized person is present at the Virtual Court Point. Sub-rule (9) requires the Virtual Assistants at both ends to ensure compliance with the minimum facilities prescribed under Rule 5. Under sub-rule (1 1), the Virtual Assistant at the Virtual Court Point must ensure the presence of the relevant participants Iifteen minutes before the scheduled proceedings, familiarize them with the platform and equipment, arrange a test call where requested, ensure that only permitted devices are brought or used and restrict entry to authorized persons' The provision also contemplates appropriate arrangements for communication between the parties and their counsel before the hearing, where permitted by the Court. These requirements are intended to ensure that the proceedings commence in an orderly manner and that the witness is not exposed to any unauthorized assistance or interference.

35. Rule 6(12) further prescribes the responsibilities of the Virtual Assistant at the Court Point, including ensuring reliable internet connectivity, coordination between both locations, proper communication, the presence and participation of authorized persons only, adequate lighting and compliance with the technical requirements' The Virtual Assistant is also required to provide feedback to the Court regarding the quality of the conference, including any objection concerning poor audio or video quality' Sub-rule (16) requires that any diffrculty or intern:ption in connectivity or communication be immediately brought to the notice of the Court for appropriate directions' These provisions collectively establishthattheVirtua]Assistantisnotmerelyatechnical operator but performs an important supervisory and facilitative function under the directions of the Court' 36. Rule 7 deals with the service of Court processes' Sub-rule (1) requires that the process issued to a proposed person for virtual proceedings specify the time, date and place of the relevant Virtual Court Point and direct the person to attend in person along with proof of identity' The ordinary provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, concerning service of Court processes and the consequences of non-attendance continue to apply, mutatis mutandis. Although this provision is not directly determinative of the objection raised in the present petition, it reinforces the requirement that a witness participating through a video link must appear at an identifred and authorized location and remain Subject to the authority of tJ.e Court.

37. Rule 8 prescribes the procedure for conducting virtual hearings. Under sub-rules (2) and (3), the Virtual Assistant at the Court Point must ensure that the proceedings are conducted through the platform directed by the Court and that they take place at the scheduled date and time. Of particular importance is sub-rule (5), which requires the person to be examined to confirm his or her identity before taking the oath and produce an identity document issued or recognized by the Government of Pakistan or the competent authority concerned. Under sub-rule (6), the opposite part5r must be provided with a copy of the identity document of the person to be examined, whereas sub-rule (7) requires the Court, !\rith the assistance of the Virtual Assistant at the Virtual Court Point, to confirm the identity of the person appearing or being examined and reflect such verifrcation in the order sheet. Thus, identity verifrcation is not to remain an informal exercise; it must form part of the judicial record.

38. Rule 8(9) restricts the persons who may remain present in the room where virtual proceedings are conducted. Except with the permission of the Court, only the parties, their representatives, advocates and persons being examined or heard may be present. Photography, broadcasting, video recording, audio recording, electronic recording, frlming and streaming of proceedings are also prohibited, except where expressly permitted by the Court. Sub-rule (10) prohibits the participation of any other person after commencement of the proceedings without the Court's permission. These restrictions are designed to preserve the solemnity, conhdentiality and independence of judicial proceedings. They assume particular importance where a witness is appearing from another judicial establishment and the defence has raised an objection that some unidentified person may be influencing her testimony.

39. Rule 8(11) further empowers the Court to order multi-point virtual proceedings through a conference between the Court, the witrqess and the other party or his advocate, where the relevant persons are available at different locations. This provision facilitates the recording of evidence while ensuring that the parties remain connected to the proceedings and are afforded an opportunity to participate effectively. It also demonstrates that the Rules contemplate a judicially controlled arrangement rather than a unilateral or informal communication between the witness and the Court. 4o. Rule 9 specifically governs the examination of persons and constitutes the most relevant provision for resolving the controversy involved in the present petition. Under sub-rule (1), the person to be examined must conlirm his or her identity in accordance with Rule 8(5), while sub-rule (2) provides that the Virtual Assistant at the Court Point shall, under the direction of the Court, administer the oath to the person being examined. Sub-rule (3) imposes specific obligations upon the Court during the examination. It requires the Court to ensure that the proceedings are recorded in a transcript that preserves their accuracy and credibility, record the demeanour of the person examined, determine objections after affording adequate opportunity of hearing to the parties, obtain the signature of the person examined on the transcript where required by law, protect the privacy of vulnerable persons and impose any other conditions necessary for the effective recording of the examination.

41. Rule 9(4) is decisive for the present controversy. It places an express obligation upon the Virtual Assistant at the Virtual Court Point to ensure that the person being examined does not refer to any document, script or device without the permission of the concerned Court. More importantly, clause (b) expressly provides that the witness must not be prompted, tutored, coaxed, induced or coerced in any manner by any person, nor should he or she seek or be provided any support in any form to manoeuvre the examination, except where leading questions in examination-in-chief are permissible under the law or where a witness is confronted with a document in accordance with law. The language of this provision leaves no ambiguity regarding the obligation to preserve the independence of the testimony. The prohibition is not confrned to actual tutoring; it extends to prompting, coaxing, inducement, coercion and any form of assistance .intended to influence or manipulate the examination.
42. The combined effect of Rule 9(3) and ( )

is that the responsibility for ensuring an independent examination is shared between the Court and the Virtual Assistant at the remote location. The Court must observe the demeanour of the witness, consider objections and impose appropriate conditions, while the Virtual Assistant must ensure that the witness is not receiving unauthorized assistance or consulting any material or device without permission. Consequently, where the defence specifically alleges that a witness is being prompted or assisted during the recording of evidence, the objection cannot be treated as a mere technical complaint. It directly attracts the safeguards expressly prescribed under Rule 9 and requires an appropriate judicial determination.

43. Rule 10 deals with the exhibiting or displaying of documents to witnesses or accused persons at the Virtual Court Point. It provides for the transmission and display of relevant documents through authorized electronic means and, where required, the countersigning of hard copies by the witness and the Virtual Assistant. The provision is relevant because Rule 9(4)(a) prohibits the witness from referring to any document, script or device without the permission of the Court. Therefore, a distinction must be maintained between documents lawfully shown to a witness by the Court for the purpose of examination and unauthorized material being consulted by the witness for the purpose of receiving assistance or preparing answers.

44. Rule 1 1 regulates the transcript of examination and prescribes the procedure for obtaining the signature of the person examined. [t provides for the transmission of the transcript between the Court Point and the Virtual Court point, whether through digital signatures or signed hard copies, and requires the Virtual Assistant at the remote location to transmit the signed transcript to the Court Point in the prescribed manner. The provision also requires the Virtual Assistant to record the refusal of the person examined to sign the transcript, where such a situation arises. The transcript, therefore, forms an important part of the judicial record and provides an additional safeguard regarding the accuracy and authenticity of the evidence recorded through virtual means.

45. Rule 12 deals with ensuring seamless virtual Court proceedings. Under sub-rule (1), the Court regulates the establishment and disconnection of the Real-time Link between the Court Point and the Virtual Court Point. Sub-rule (2) specifically requires the Court, before commencement of the virtual hearing, to satisfy itself that all participants and the Court can be seen and heard clearly and distinctly. The requirement is not merely technical. Clear audio and video transmission is essential for observing the witness, recording her demeanour, understanding her answers and enabling the parties to conduct effective cross-examination. Any technical deficiency affecting these requirements must be rectified before the proceedings continue.

46. Rule 13 identifies certain proceedings which may be conducted virtually, subject to the restrictions contained therein. Although the Court may, at its discretion, authorize certain proceedings relating to judicial remand and framing of charge through virtual means, sub-rule (2) expressly prohibits the examination of a witness under section 164 Cr.P.C., the examination of an accused under sections 164 and 364 Cr.P.C. and the recording of the statement of an accused under section 342 Cr.P.C. through virtual Court proceedings. The distinction is important because the Rules permit tJ.e virtual examination of witnesses in ordinary criminal proceedings but expressly preserve the statutory safeguards applicable to the specified categories of statements.

47. Rule 14 prescribes the conduct and responsibilities of participants in virtual proceedings. It requires all users, whether physicatly or virtually present, to observe the solemnity of judicial proceedings and comply with the directions of the Court and the Virtual Assistant. It also regulates the conduct of advocates and other participants during the hearing. These requirements reinforce the principle that virtual proceedings are judicial proceedings and must maintain the same dignity, discipline and decorum as proceedings conducted in a physical courtroom.

48. Rules 15 to 18 deal with costs, training, removal of difficulties and residual matters. Rule 15 regulates the costs of virtual proceedings; Rule 16 enables the High Court to arrange training for Judges, lawyers and relevant officials regarding the operation of video-conferencing equipment and modern devices; Rule 17 empowers the High Court to remove diffrculties and relax the Rules in appropriate cases; and Rule 18 provides that matters not expressly covered by the Rules shall be dealt with by the Court in the exercise of its discretion, as may be necessary to secure the ends of justice or prevent abuse of the process of the Court. These provisions complete the procedural framework and demonstrate that the Rules are intended to provide an effective and comprehensive mechanism for the conduct of virtual proceedings.

49. A cumulative reading of the above provisions makes it clear that the Rules do not treat the virtual examination of a witness as a mere electronic transmission of evidence. Rather, they prescribe a complete procedural mechanism involving prior judicial permission, identification of the witness, designation of authorized Virtual Assistants, supervision at both locations, regulation of the persons and devices permitted at the remote Iocation, observation of the witness's demeanour, prevention of prompting or tutoring, determination of objections, preparation of an authenticated transcript and maintenance of clear and uninterrupted communication. These requirements are intended to ensure that the use of technologr facilitates the administration of justice without undermining the independence and credibility of evidence.

t9 50. In the present case, the prosecution witness was permitted to record her statement through video conferencing from the Court of the learned District and Sessions Judge, Peshawar. Such an arrangement is not inherently unlawful, as Rule 6 read with Schedule-B expressly recognizes the possibility of examination of a witness from a Court falling within the jurisdiction of another district. However, the arrangement must satisfy the requirements of the Rules, particularly the nomination of an authorized Virtual Assistant by the concerned District and Sessions Judge. The mere presence of the witness within the premises .of a judicial establishment is not sufficient to establish compliance with this requirement. The learned trial Court must ascertain whether the person supervising the witness at the remote location was duly authorized and whether the procedural safeguards prescribed under Rules 6, 8 and 9 had been observed.

51. The initial permission to record the complainant's statement through video conferencing was granted without objection from the defence. Such consent is a relevant circumstance, but it cannot be treated as an irrevocable waiver of the accused's right to object to any subsequent irregularity arising during the recording of evidence. The duty of the trial Court to ensure a fair and la*{ul recording of evidence continues throughout the proceedings. Once the defence raised a specific objection that the witness appeared to be receiving instructions or prompting from unidentified persons, the learned trial Court was required to examine the objection in the light of Rule 9(3)(c) and Rule 9(4) of the Rules' 5l2. It is equally important to observe that an allegation of prompting cannot be accepted as established merely because the witness appeared on the screen or because the defence entertained an apprehension regarding her conduct' The objection must be examined objectively. The learned trial Court may require the Virtual Assistant at the remote location to confirm whether any other person was present, whether the witness had access to any document, script or electronic device and whether any circumstance existed which influenced her answers. The Court may also could require have the witness's immediate surroundings to be displayed through the carnera, to the extent reasonably necessary, and impose such additional conditions as may be required under Rule 9(3)(f).

53. The mere fact that the witness was appearing from the premises of another Court cannot be treated as conclusive proof that no outside influence was possible. Equally, the possibility of prompting cannot be presumed solely because the witness is not physically present before the trial Judge. The Rules have specifically provided a mechanism to address such concerns through the presence of an authorized Virtual Assistant and the supervisory powers of the Court. The learned trial Court must, therefore, determine the objection on the basis of the circumstances established before it and not merely on the basis of the location from which the witness is appearing.

54. The right of cross-examination is not satisfied merely by allowing counsel to put questions through a video link. The arrangement must enable counsel to hear the answers clearly, observe the witness and challenge her testimony without technical or'procedural obstruction. Rule 9(3)(b), which requires the Court to record the demeanour of the person examined, and Rule 12(21, which requires the Court to satisfy itself that the participants can be seen and heard clearly and distinctly, are intended to preserve the effectiveness of this process. If the connection is interrupted, if the witness cannot be properly observed or if a reasonable apprehension of outside influence arises, the Court must address the issue and pass an appropriate order.

55. The learned trial Court, while refusing the request for physical appearance, principally relied upon the fact that the witness was present in the Court of the learned District and Sessions Judge, Peshawar, under judicial supervision. Although this circumstance supports the suitability of the remote location, it does not, by itself, answer the speci{ic objection raised by the defence regarding possible prompting. The learned trial Court was required to examine whether the requirements of Rule 6 and Schedule-B had been fulfilled and whether the 2t safeguards expressly prescribed under Rule 9 were being observed.

56. At the same time, the petitioner cannot claim an absolute right to insist upon the physical appearance of the witness merely because her evidence is being recorded through video conferencing. The Rules expressly recoglize the virtual examination of witnesses, and physical appearance is not an infledble requirement in every case. The appropriate mode must be determined in the light of the circumstances of the case, the availability of the prescribed safeguards and the necessity of ensuring a fair trial. Where the safeguards can effectively secure the independence of the testimony and the accused's right of cross-examination, the continuation of virtual proceedings cannot be objected to merely on the ground that the witness is situated at another judicial establishment.

57. In the circumstances, this Court is not inclined to declare the video-link arrangement unlawful or to direct the physical production of the witness as an automatic consequence of the objection raised by the defence. However, the impugned order calnot be treated as relieving the learned trial Court of its obligation to ensure compliance with the statutory provisions and the Peshawar High Court Virtual Court Proceedings Rules, 2026. The learned trial Court must specifically address the objection raised by the defence and ensure that the safeguards prescribed under the Rules are observed before proceeding with the remaining crossexamination.
58. Consequently, this petition is disposed of with the following directions:
